strapline: A K284.8 billion budget with VAT at 16.5% and a tax on mining dividends; rail money and a power line to Tanzania; the RDAZ president is retired; Blades back on top

stories.title: K284.8 billion and half a point on VAT: Musokotwane's 2027 budget taxes mining dividends at 15%, adds a 39.5% PAYE band and aims the deficit at 3% of GDP
stories.excerpt: The Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, presented a K284.8 billion budget for 2027 to the National Assembly on Friday 6 November, the largest in Zambia's history and 28.4% of GDP. Domestic revenue is to cover K233.7 billion of it, borrowing K41.9 billion and grants K9.2 billion. VAT rises from 16% to 16.5%, a 15% withholding tax lands on mining company dividends, a new 39.5% PAYE band applies to monthly pay above K37,000, and debt service alone takes K67.6 billion.

image.label: The 2027 budget
image.caption: Zambia's 2027 budget is K284.8 billion, 82% of it from domestic revenue, with VAT rising to 16.5% and a new tax on mining dividends.

body: Zambia's 2027 budget is K284.8 billion, up from K253.1 billion this year and equal to 28.4% of GDP, and it is to be paid for largely by Zambians themselves: Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 6 November that the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, told the National Assembly that domestic revenue of K233.7 billion would cover 82.1% of spending, with K41.9 billion of domestic and external borrowing (14.7%) and K9.2 billion of grants making up the rest. The budget's theme is "Grow Zambia: From Stabilisation to Unlocking Opportunities, Creating Jobs and Improving Livelihoods for All", and the Monitor reported that the new tax measures are expected to raise K10.8 billion.

The tax measures, all effective from 1 January 2027 according to Zambia Monitor, start with the headline consumption tax: value added tax rises from 16% to 16.5%. On income, a new 39.5% PAYE band applies to monthly earnings above K37,000. Mining companies, which have paid no withholding tax on dividends, will pay 15%, and a 5% export duty is introduced on zinc concentrates. In the other direction, the mineral royalty on gold that artisanal miners sell to approved aggregators falls from 6% to 3%, customs duty and VAT are suspended on imported raw materials for making sanitary products, and import duties rise on ceramic tiles, selected aluminium products and processed meat to shelter local producers. Briefs, a finance site reporting from Bloomberg's account of the speech, confirmed the VAT increase and the 15% mining dividend levy.

The Zambian Observer, in a first reaction by the Socialist Party president, Fred M'membe, listed further measures that the other pages read for this edition did not itemise: higher mobile money levies in every band, a new tax of K1 per kilogram on sugar, and higher passport and civil registration fees. Those three items rest on that single account and are noted as such below.

The largest function is general public services at K90.5 billion, or 31.8% of the budget, which The Zambian Observer, carrying a Phoenix FM report, said includes K67.6 billion for debt service, K4.7 billion for dismantling arrears and K1.7 billion for digitalising government services. A second Observer report, on the reaction of the Bwana Mkubwa MP Warren Chisha Mwambazi, put education at K38.2 billion and health at K30.3 billion, with 3,125 health workers to be recruited and six universities to be built; K18.1 billion for building, upgrading and rehabilitating 787 kilometres of road; and the Constituency Development Fund rising from K6.2 billion to about K9 billion while the K40 million per constituency stays the same. The same report said the Farmer Input Support Programme becomes an agricultural loan scheme in 2027 and that a K5 billion loan guarantee scheme is proposed for small businesses. Mr M'membe's statement said the Social Cash Transfer rises by K50 to K450 a month.

body.title: The 2027 budget in figures
items: K284.8 billion total, 28.4% of GDP (K253.1 billion in 2026)
K233.7 billion domestic revenue, K41.9 billion borrowing, K9.2 billion grants
VAT 16% to 16.5%; new 39.5% PAYE band above K37,000 a month
15% withholding tax on mining dividends; 5% export duty on zinc concentrates
K67.6 billion debt service; K38.2 billion education; K30.3 billion health
Deficit target 3% of GDP in 2027, from an expected 5.9% this year

body.text: The deficit and the copper behind it

body: Briefs reported, citing Bloomberg, that the 2026 deficit is now expected at 5.9% of GDP against a 2.1% target, that the 2027 target is 3%, and that the plan narrows it to 1.2% by 2029. The gap widened, in that account, because spending rose even as near-record copper prices lifted revenue: the government shielded households from the fuel price surge linked to the Iran war and, in an election year, bought maize from farmers at five times the volume first intended. Copper topped US$14,000 a tonne this year; output is projected at 930,000 tonnes in 2026, short of the one-million-tonne goal, with targets of more than one million tonnes in 2027 and 1.4 million in 2029. Briefs said meeting the deficit goal is "key to securing final approval" of the IMF-backed programme.

The Zambia Daily Mail, previewing the speech on Friday morning, set out the Grow Zambia targets the budget is meant to serve: three million tonnes of copper a year, ten million tonnes of maize, 10,000 megawatts of generation capacity and five million tourist arrivals by 2031. News Diggers reported the same morning that the budget came amid calls for jobs, tax relief and a lower cost of living, and that Parliament had just approved a K19.9 billion supplementary budget, about K14 billion of it to pay farmers owed for maize delivered to the Food Reserve Agency.
Mr Mwambazi, according to the Observer, welcomed the loan guarantee scheme as a route to entrepreneurship and jobs, and said the test was delivery.

body.text: The success of these commitments will depend on effective implementation, responsible use of public resources
body.attribution: Warren Chisha Mwambazi, MP for Bwana Mkubwa, in remarks reported by The Zambian Observer on 6 November

body: Mr M'membe took the opposite view of the same numbers. He said that one kwacha in every four goes to debt, that the K67.6 billion for lenders is more than double the health allocation, and that VAT, the mobile money levies and the sugar tax fall on everyone regardless of income. He welcomed the mining dividend tax, but called it late.

body.text: This step is overdue, and it is small.
body.attribution: Fred M'membe, Socialist Party president, in a statement published by The Zambian Observer on 6 November

body: His overall verdict was that the budget "serves the lenders and the investors first, and ordinary Zambians last". The government's case, as Zambia Monitor reported it, is that fiscal sustainability has been the UPND's strategic focus since it came to office and that the budget is built to accelerate development while keeping discipline. The Monitor quoted the opening of the minister's sentence on that point: "One of the UPND's strategic focus since coming into Government has been to strengthen fiscal sustainability".

body.confirmed: The totals (K284.8 billion; K233.7 billion revenue; K41.9 billion borrowing; K9.2 billion grants), the VAT rise to 16.5%, the 15% withholding tax on mining dividends, the 39.5% PAYE band and the 1 January start date (Zambia Monitor; the totals and the two main tax changes also in The Zambian Observer and in Briefs citing Bloomberg). Debt service of K67.6 billion, education K38.2 billion and health K30.3 billion (two Zambian Observer reports). The 3% deficit target and the 5.9% expected outturn for 2026 (Briefs, citing Bloomberg).
body.unverified: The mobile money levy increases, the K1 per kilogram sugar tax and higher passport and registration fees rest on Fred M'membe's statement as published by The Zambian Observer and were not itemised on any other page read for this edition. Growth and inflation targets, the full list of sector allocations and the financing split between domestic and external borrowing were not on the pages read; Lusaka Times, ZNBC and Mwebantu reports on the speech could not be opened. The budget speech itself had not been published on a government page found during this run.

stories.title: €60 million for Kapiri Mposhi–Ndola and the 1984 Railways Act to go: the budget opens the line to private trains, as Wonderful Group talks of US$1.2 billion for the southern line
stories.excerpt: The 2027 budget speech carried the first firm money for Zambia Railways in some time: an initial €60 million to rehabilitate the Kapiri Mposhi–Ndola section, reported by Zambia Monitor, with Zambia Railways to become an infrastructure manager and freight and passenger services opened to private operators. A day earlier, the Zambia Daily Mail reported that the Wonderful Group of Companies intends to put more than US$1.2 billion into rehabilitating the Livingstone–Chililabombwe line to move its cargo off the roads.

image.label: Open access rail
image.caption: The budget promises €60 million for the Kapiri Mposhi–Ndola line and a new Railways Act that lets private operators run trains.

body: Railways had a day on Friday 6 November. Zambia Monitor reported that the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, told Parliament in the budget speech that Zambia had secured an initial €60 million to rehabilitate the Kapiri Mposhi–Ndola section of the national railway, and that the government was engaging other partners to fund the remaining sections of the Zambia Railways network. The Monitor's report did not name the lender.

The structural change matters as much as the money. According to the Monitor, Zambia Railways Limited is to become the railway infrastructure manager, with freight and passenger train services opened to private operators under an open access model, and the minister said the government would "repeal and replace the Railways Act Cap 453 of 1984" to improve operational efficiency and sustainable infrastructure financing. The speech, as reported, also placed the start of construction on the Lobito railway line in the fourth quarter of 2027, said rehabilitation of the TAZARA line was under way, and promised a dry port at Kapiri Mposhi. Mr Musokotwane tied all of it to exports: "The Grow Zambia Agenda must be led by expansion in exports."

The same report listed the road and air works the budget funds: 787 kilometres of roads to be built, upgraded or rehabilitated; works already begun on the Mutanda–Kisasa–Mwinilunga–Jimbe road and on the Kasempa turn-off to Kabompo via Mufumbwe; Mansa and Mfuwe airports to be completed in 2027; and continuing work at Nakonde airport. The minister said border operations were being modernised with the private sector: "Government, working with the private sector, is modernising border operations to speed up trade processing."

body.text: A private bid for the southern line

body: The Zambia Daily Mail reported on Friday morning, from Chilanga, that the Wonderful Group of Companies plans to invest slightly more than US$1.2 billion in rehabilitating the Livingstone–Chililabombwe railway line, to shift part of its cargo from road to rail. The company's chief executive disclosed the plan during a tour of the group's industrial park on Thursday 5 November by senior public servants led by the Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet for Finance and Economic Development, Siazongo Siakalenge. The Daily Mail said the group moves its products on about 1,000 trucks a day, and that Mr Siakalenge said the investment would take pressure off the road network.

Mr Siakalenge used the visit to make a point about the civil service. The Daily Mail reported that he cited the eight months Wonderful Group waited to be granted industrial park status as an example of how slow administrative decisions hold back investment, and said the tour would help permanent secretaries identify legislation that industry finds problematic.

body.text: Having appreciated what is happening on the ground, permanent secretaries will be well positioned to put in effort
body.attribution: Siazongo Siakalenge, Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet for Finance and Economic Development, at the Wonderful Group industrial park on 5 November, quoted by the Zambia Daily Mail

body: Neither report gave a timetable for the Wonderful Group project, said whether it had been agreed with the government or Zambia Railways, or explained how a private rehabilitation of the Livingstone–Chililabombwe line would fit the open access model announced in the budget. No statement from Zambia Railways on either announcement was found on the pages read for this edition.

stories.title: Two contracts signed, 386 kilometres of line, power by 2029: Kapala tells Parliament the Tanzania interconnector is under way, and promises no load shedding, El Niño or not
stories.excerpt: The Minister of Electricity, Peter Kapala, told the National Assembly on Thursday 5 November that Zambia's 613-kilometre share of the Zambia–Tanzania–Kenya interconnector will be commissioned in the second quarter of 2029 and will let Zambia trade up to 500 megawatts. Ecofin Agency reported that the first two of five packages, the Pensulo–Mpika and Mpika–Kasama lines, were awarded to China's Sinotec consortium on 19 October. News Diggers reported his assurance that there will be no load shedding whatever the coming rains bring.

image.label: 613 km to Nakonde
image.caption: Zambia's section of the interconnector runs from Pensulo through Mpika and Kasama to Nakonde, with commissioning planned for 2029.

body: The transmission line that is meant to join southern Africa's power pool to east Africa's has moved from memoranda to contractors. In a ministerial statement to Parliament on Thursday 5 November, reported by Zambia Monitor, the Minister of Electricity, Peter Kapala, said Zambia's portion of the Zambia–Tanzania Interconnector, about 613 kilometres of line and associated works from Pensulo in Serenje district through Mpika and Kasama to Nakonde, is expected to be completed within 24 months and commissioned in the second quarter of 2029.

Ecofin Agency, reporting on Friday 6 November, said the minister told Parliament that the first two construction contracts, for the Pensulo–Mpika and Mpika–Kasama lines, were awarded on 19 October to China's Sinotec consortium, which began detailed site surveys on 2 November. Together they cover 386 kilometres of 330-kilovolt line. The remaining packages are the Kasama–Nakonde lines, a new substation at Nakonde, for which procurement is expected to conclude by March 2027, and voltage-support equipment at the Pensulo and Nakonde substations. ZESCO is implementing the project.

The money is in place, in grants rather than loans. Zambia Monitor and Ecofin both reported US$292 million secured for the Zambian section: US$245 million from the World Bank's International Development Association, US$30 million from the European Union and US$17 million from the United Kingdom, under a grant facility agreement signed on 29 January 2025 that became effective on 25 April 2025. The wider corridor, about 2,300 kilometres linking Zambia, Tanzania and Kenya under a tripartite memorandum signed in December 2014, is estimated at US$1.2 billion, with each country financing and building the section in its own territory.

body.text: The Zambia-Tanzania Interconnector is a strategic project to the Grow Zambia Agenda
body.attribution: Peter Kapala, Minister of Electricity, in a ministerial statement to the National Assembly on 5 November, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: Mr Kapala said the line would allow Zambia to trade up to 500 megawatts and help make the country a regional power-trading hub, and he asked MPs and stakeholders to support the government in implementing it.

News Diggers led its report on the same statement with a different line: that with or without El Niño there will be no load shedding. The paper reported that Mr Kapala assured citizens there would be no power rationing despite the anticipated El Niño pattern, and that the interconnector was part of the government's effort to strengthen supply. Ecofin noted the background to that promise: ZESCO's 2025 integrated report puts generation at 8,739 gigawatt-hours in 2025, up from 7,469 in 2024, after the 2024 drought cut reservoir levels and brought shortages and load shedding, while export revenue fell to K5 billion in 2025 from K7.2 billion the year before. The Diggers report was partly behind a paywall; the figures on which the no-load-shedding assurance rests were not on the part of the page that could be read.

stories.title: A million hectares and more than US$100 million: the government asks the World Bank to hurry the Lobito Corridor forest project, with first activities pencilled in for January
stories.excerpt: The Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame, urged a World Bank delegation in Lusaka on Thursday 5 November to speed up the design of the Lobito Corridor Integrated Forest Economy (LIFE) Project so that an agreement can be signed, Zambia Monitor reported. News Diggers reported a day earlier that the ministry's Permanent Secretary, Douty Chibamba, put the cost of the one-million-hectare plantation scheme at more than US$100 million and said preliminary work should start in January 2027.

image.label: The LIFE project
image.caption: The government and the World Bank are designing a forestry project along the Lobito Corridor meant to create jobs and local timber processing.

body: The forestry project that the government wants to run along the Lobito Corridor now has a name, a rough price and a target date, but not yet an agreement. Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 6 November that the Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame, met a World Bank Group delegation at his office in Lusaka on Thursday and asked the Bank to accelerate the design of the Lobito Corridor Integrated Forest Economy (LIFE) Project.

body.text: We need to accelerate the design and outline of the LIFE Project so that we can conclude the project agreement
body.attribution: Gilbert Siame, Minister of Green Economy and Environment, meeting a World Bank delegation in Lusaka on 5 November, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: As the Monitor described it, LIFE is envisaged as a phased, private sector-led scheme to build a sustainable forestry economy: plantations, outgrower arrangements, domestic processing and market development, with stronger forest management alongside. The delegation was led by the World Bank's country manager for Zambia, Martine Valcin, who said a recent joint exploratory mission to the Copperbelt had given the government and the Bank "a clearer understanding of how they can collaborate". The Bank's lead natural resources specialist for eastern and southern Africa, Laurent Debroux, said several companies visited on that mission were already planning to expand their plantations and invest in value addition, and a colleague, Andrew Zakharenka, said the delegation would meet the Forestry Department the following week to agree the project design before the agreement is finalised.

News Diggers reported from Ndola on Thursday 5 November that the government needs more than US$100 million to establish a one-million-hectare forestry project along the corridor in partnership with the World Bank. The ministry's Permanent Secretary, Douty Chibamba, speaking on Wednesday during a visit to ZAFFICO's operations, where a delegation assessed the company's forestry and timber-processing capacity, said resources were being mobilised from various contributors and that preliminary activities were expected to begin in January 2027. He said the government wanted rural communities along the corridor to benefit directly. The rest of the Diggers report, including Mr Chibamba's remarks on ZAFFICO's difficulties, was behind a paywall.

The Monitor's report also recorded a related launch: the Miombo Thrive movement, launched on Friday at the Pamodzi Hotel in Lusaka, which aims to turn landscape restoration into livelihoods. SNV's country director for Zambia and Zimbabwe, Lucy Fulgence, said the movement "seeks to change how landscape challenges are addressed by connecting conservation with livelihoods". The miombo woodlands, the Monitor noted, cover an estimated 2.7 million square kilometres and support more than 300 million people.

Neither report gave the financing split between the government, the Bank and private investors, the location of the first plantations, or the terms on which communities would take part. The budget speech on Friday placed the start of construction on the Lobito railway itself in the fourth quarter of 2027.

stories.title: 'You are wasting your time': Kalaba takes the EU observers' report and tells them to find a way to enforce it, as the church monitors say their own findings match the mission's
stories.excerpt: The EU Election Observation Mission has begun handing its final report to the parties. Citizens First president Harry Kalaba received it in Lusaka and, Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 6 November, agreed with its findings on ZNBC airtime, the campaign timetable and police conduct. The Zambian Observer, citing Zambian Watch, reported that he also told the observers they were wasting their time without an enforcement mechanism. The Christian Churches Monitoring Group told News Diggers its conclusions were similar to the EU's.

image.label: Thirteen recommendations
image.caption: The EU observers' final report on the 13 August election is being presented to political parties, and the opposition is asking what happens next.

body: Two days after the government said the EU observers could not see what the police could, the mission's final report on the 13 August 2026 general election is being delivered party by party, and the first opposition leader to receive it has accepted it with a condition. Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 6 November that the EU Election Observation Mission handed its report to Citizens First in Lusaka and that the party's president, Harry Kalaba, backed its findings and said the recommendations should be used to strengthen future elections.

According to the Monitor, Mr Kalaba singled out the report's finding that ZNBC gave 96.2% of its television airtime to the ruling party, which he said undermined fairness; the ECZ campaign timetable, which the report said created unequal conditions and which he said should be reviewed; and the alleged police bias and cadreism that he said constrained opposition campaigning. He also pointed to the suspension of vote counting and the closure of courts during the election period: "Those incidents raised questions about transparency and access to justice during the election period," the Monitor quoted him as saying. Citizens First, the paper said, plans to engage stakeholders on implementing the recommendations, including turning ZNBC into a genuine public service broadcaster.

body.text: And what he said to the observers

body: The Zambian Observer carried a sharper version of the same meeting, crediting an interview with Zambian Watch. In that account Mr Kalaba told the mission that observers had been producing reports and recommendations on Zambia's elections since 1996 and that many of the same concerns persisted; that "election observation should not end with the publication of reports"; and that the observers "were wasting their time if they could not find practical ways of ensuring that their recommendations are enforced". The Observer's report quoted him warning that "without practical enforcement mechanisms, election observation reports risk becoming routine documents".

News Diggers reported on Friday that the Christian Churches Monitoring Group, which fielded its own observers, says its findings are similar to the EU's. The group's programme director, Peter Mwanangombe, told the paper in an interview on Wednesday that CCMG agreed with the EU's concerns about shrinking democratic space, restrictions on political activity and human rights around the election. The remainder of his remarks was behind a paywall.

The government's position, as News Diggers restated it, is that the EU does not have access to the intelligence, security information and law-enforcement investigations available to sovereign state institutions. Lusaka Brief reported on Wednesday 4 November that the final report made 13 recommendations and that the Chief Government Spokesperson had replied that observers cannot see what the police can. No government response to Mr Kalaba's or CCMG's remarks had been published on the pages read for this edition.

sources.title: Kalaba backs EU election report, calls for reforms ahead of future polls

stories.title: Three wards voted and the UPND took all three, eight contests never happened, and the President held his first rally since August: what Thursday's by-elections produced
stories.excerpt: Of the 14 by-elections the Electoral Commission scheduled for Thursday 5 November, eight could not be held after candidates withdrew, News Diggers reported; in three of the wards that did vote, Lwingishi in Mansa, Lubaleshi in Kanchibiya and Mbeta in Sioma, The Zambian Observer reported UPND wins by margins of 700, 1,960 and 163 votes. In Mandevu, where the parliamentary contest collapsed, President Hichilema held his first public rally since the general election and introduced the MP declared without a poll, the Zambia Daily Mail reported.

image.label: Three wards, three wins
image.caption: The UPND won the Lwingishi, Lubaleshi and Mbeta ward by-elections on 5 November; eight other contests were not held.

body: The by-election day that was to have included two parliamentary seats and a mayoralty ended up being decided in a handful of council wards. News Diggers reported on Friday 6 November that of the 14 by-elections the Electoral Commission of Zambia had set for Thursday 5 November, two parliamentary (Lumezi North and Mandevu), the Mbala mayoral contest and 12 council wards, eight could not be held: both parliamentary seats, the mayoralty and five wards, after candidate withdrawals left single candidates standing. In five wards, the paper said, only the UPND successfully filed nominations.

The Zambian Observer reported three results on Friday. In Lwingishi ward in Mansa district, the UPND's James Mwandu polled 1,832 votes to 1,132 for Chanda Chimba of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP); an earlier Observer report, which spelt the winner's surname Mwando, put the total votes cast at 3,039 with 55 rejected ballots from 5,974 registered voters. In Lubaleshi ward in Kanchibiya district, Nelson Bwalya of the UPND took 2,327 votes against 367 for Katongo Lupupa of the NRP and 249 for Doris Chintu of Citizens First. In Mbeta ward in Sioma district, Situmbeko Yuyi of the UPND won 522 votes to 359 for the independent Mwanamwalye Mwanamwalye. The Observer's reports did not give turnout for the second and third wards or name the returning officers.

body.title: Thursday's ward results, as reported by The Zambian Observer
items: Lubaleshi (Kanchibiya): Bwalya, UPND, 2,327; Lupupa, NRP, 367; Chintu, CF, 249

body: ECZ Commissioner Zevyanji Sinkala, who toured six of the ten polling stations in Lwingishi, commended voters, candidates and the police for keeping the peace, News Diggers reported, and said that democracy demands that citizens be given the chance to vote for their leaders. The rest of the Commission's remarks were behind the paper's paywall.

In Mandevu, where Adrian Banda was declared MP on Thursday after three opposition candidates withdrew, the President held what the Zambia Daily Mail called his first public event since the general election. The paper reported that Mr Hichilema thanked voters for re-electing him and the UPND on 13 August, introduced Mr Banda, and promised action on the constituency's water supply, roads and security. He said water was a basic necessity needing urgent action, voiced concern about insecurity caused by people commonly called junkies, directed the security wings to help the young people involved, and linked skills training for them to the enhanced Constituency Development Fund.

body.text: On August 13, you elected me and the UPND. We are ready to work for you,
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema at a rally in Mandevu on 5 November, quoted by the Zambia Daily Mail

body: News Diggers reported from the same engagement that the President told the nominated MPs present that they held their seats because of the UPND government and Bill 7, and should get out into their communities and work, and that he urged Mr Banda to stay humble. Lusaka Brief reported on Friday that the Lusaka Province Minister, Obvious Mwaliteta, had denied warning the Tonse candidate off the Mandevu race and that a judicial review of the Commission's handling of the seat, brought by Kasonde Mwenda, was before the High Court; no ruling on that application was reported on the pages read for this edition.

stories.title: Two more dates: Archbishop Banda's Hilux case goes to 25 November while the DPP answers a defence application, and the treason bail panel is reported to rule on 10 November
stories.excerpt: The Archdiocese of Lusaka said on Friday that the case against Archbishop Alick Banda, charged with possessing a Toyota Hilux suspected of being unlawfully obtained, has been adjourned to Wednesday 25 November, with the Director of Public Prosecutions to respond to a defence application and the defence to reply by 18 November, ACI Africa and The Zambian Observer reported. The Observer also reported that the High Court panel hearing the bail petition of Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others will rule on the State's objection on 10 November.

image.label: 25 November, 10 November
image.caption: The Archbishop's trial and the treason bail petition both left the Lusaka courts on Friday with new dates and no decisions.

body: Neither of the two Lusaka cases that had Friday 6 November in their diaries produced a decision. The trial of Archbishop Alick Banda, which had already been put off on Tuesday when the prosecution did not appear, now has a date three weeks away, and the bail petition of the 18 treason accused has, according to one outlet, a ruling date on a point of procedure.

ACI Africa reported on Friday that the Archdiocese of Lusaka said in a statement that the case "has been adjourned to Wednesday, 25th November 2026". The prosecution, led by the Director of Public Prosecutions, is to respond to an application filed by the defence, and the defence is to make its subsequent response by 18 November. The Zambian Observer carried the same dates and the same sequence. Neither report described what the defence application asks for or named the magistrate.

The charge, as ACI Africa set it out, is possession of a blue Toyota Hilux, registration ALF 7734, suspected of being unlawfully obtained, between 22 April 2021 and 27 December 2023. The Drug Enforcement Commission says the vehicle belonged to the Zambia Revenue Authority and is part of a wider investigation into about 22 ZRA vehicles allegedly disposed of improperly. The Archbishop has pleaded not guilty. He was charged on 28 September and granted bail of K80,000 in his own recognisance with three working sureties of K50,000 each, surrendered his travel documents and spent one night at Chimbokaila before the bail process was completed; the case was mentioned on 14 October, and the 3 November hearing was postponed because the prosecution team did not appear.

The Zambian Observer reported on Friday that the three-judge Lusaka High Court panel hearing the constitutional bail application of the NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 16 co-accused adjourned the matter to 10 November, when it will rule on the State's preliminary objection that the application should be dismissed on procedural grounds. In the Observer's account, lead defence counsel Sakwiba Sikota argued that holding the accused without trial breached their rights to liberty and the presumption of innocence and called it "an illegal prolonged detention", while the State maintained that the offences are non-bailable and a grave matter of national security. If the objection fails, the panel would hear the bail application on its merits; if it succeeds, the application is dismissed without a hearing, and the defence has said it would challenge that outcome.

That account carries the byline of Anthony Mukwita and reads as commentary rather than a court report, and no other outlet read for this edition had reported the 10 November date; it is treated as unverified below. What the established record shows is that the panel of Judges Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga allowed the State on Thursday to raise its objection and adjourned to Friday morning, as Lusaka Brief reported yesterday; that the State's affidavit, reported by Zambia Monitor on 29 October, argues the two leaders are a flight risk with networks that could interfere with witnesses; and that Mr Zulu, as Zambia Monitor reported on Friday, has asked the court to let him conduct his own case, a step the Monitor likened to Shamwana v The People. The 18 have been in custody since August on treason and terrorism-related charges, which they deny.

body.confirmed: Archbishop Banda's case is adjourned to 25 November, with the DPP to respond to a defence application and the defence to reply by 18 November (Archdiocese of Lusaka statement, reported by ACI Africa and The Zambian Observer). The charge, the plea of not guilty and the bail terms (ACI Africa). Makebi Zulu's application to represent himself (Zambia Monitor).
body.unverified: The 10 November ruling date on the State's preliminary objection in the treason bail petition rests on a single Zambian Observer column; no court reporter's account of Friday's sitting was found. The nature of the defence application in the Archbishop's case. Whether the accused in the treason matter were brought to court on Friday.

stories.title: 'I have done nothing wrong apart from speaking for doctors': the RDAZ president is retired in the national interest, and two opposition leaders ask the Ministry of Health why
stories.excerpt: Dr Paul Chibwe, president of the Resident Doctors Association of Zambia and an orthopaedic and trauma surgeon at Levy Mwanawasa University Teaching Hospital, told News Diggers he was handed a letter retiring him early in the national interest without an explanation. The Socialist Party's Fred M'membe asked the Ministry of Health to reverse the decision, and the OPP's Brian Mushimba said the circumstances should be established. No reason from the ministry had been published on the pages read for this edition.

image.label: Retired, no reason given
image.caption: The president of the resident doctors' association says he was retired early with no explanation; the Ministry of Health has not said why.

body: The doctor who has spent the past year speaking for Zambia's unemployed and volunteer medical graduates is now out of a job himself. News Diggers reported on Friday 6 November that Dr Paul Chibwe, president of the Resident Doctors Association of Zambia (RDAZ) and an orthopaedics and trauma surgeon at Levy Mwanawasa University Teaching Hospital, had been retired in the national interest. He announced it in a Facebook post on Wednesday and told the paper in an interview on Thursday that he was simply handed a letter informing him of his early retirement, without a detailed explanation.

Dr Chibwe told News Diggers that he does not know why he was retired and that he has done nothing wrong apart from speaking for doctors. He said he was not aware of any wrongdoing on his part, and argued that if he had committed an offence, disciplinary action would have been taken against him. The rest of the interview was behind the paper's paywall; the visible portion did not name the appointing authority that signed the letter or the legal provision relied on.

The Socialist Party president, Fred M'membe, in a statement published by The Zambian Observer on Friday, said the Ministry of Health under Professor Roma Chilengi had implemented what he called a sudden retirement in the national interest, and urged the ministry to reconsider. His statement said that using administrative retirement against the leadership of professional bodies "creates a chilling effect", described Dr Chibwe as part of "a vital tier of highly specialised young medical personnel that Zambia cannot afford to lose", and placed the decision alongside what it called the mass termination of 400 staff at the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency and the redeployment of 123 Ministry of Health headquarters workers. Those two figures come from Mr M'membe's statement and were not reported separately on the pages read.

body.text: We urge the Ministry of Health to reconsider its decision regarding Dr. Chibwe.
body.attribution: Fred M'membe, Socialist Party president, in a statement published by The Zambian Observer on 6 November

body: The Organised People's Party president, Brian Mushimba, said in remarks carried by the Observer that the circumstances behind the dismissal should be established, warned against retaliation for speaking out, and asked why trained doctors remain unemployed after the public investment in their education: "How can we invest in them so much and leave them on the streets?" He said his party had employed at least 20 unemployed doctors in its secretariat before the August election and that he had helped a former RDAZ president, Dr Brian Sampa, relocate to the United States after his dismissal.

The context is a long argument between the association and the ministry over recruitment. Lusaka Brief reported last month that RDAZ had asked that hiring under the US health pact begin with the doctors already volunteering inside the system, and Friday's budget speech, as reported by The Zambian Observer, provides for 3,125 health workers to be recruited in 2027. Neither the Ministry of Health nor the Health Services Commission had given a reason for Dr Chibwe's retirement on any page read for this edition, and his letter has not been published.

stories.title: Blades back on top of Stream A a day after Nkana got there, Green Eagles two clear in Stream B with one goal conceded in six, and a goalless Lusaka derby at Sunset
stories.excerpt: Konkola Blades beat Trident 2–1 at Konkola Stadium on Thursday 5 November to retake first place in Stream A of the MTN Super League transitional season with 15 points from six, two ahead of Nkana. In Stream B, Derrick Bulaya scored twice as Green Eagles won 2–0 at Chirundu United to lead by two points, while Green Buffaloes and Zesco United drew 0–0 at Sunset Stadium. Power Dynamos beat NAPSA Stars 1–0 and Nchanga Rangers beat Makeni All Stars 3–1.

image.label: Matchweek 7, Thursday
image.caption: Konkola Blades lead Stream A and Green Eagles lead Stream B after Thursday's round of the transitional season.

body: Nkana's stay at the top of Stream A lasted a day. ZamFoot reported that Konkola Blades beat Trident FC 2–1 at Konkola Stadium on Thursday 5 November, the second half of the midweek round, to return to first place with 15 points from six matches, five wins and one defeat, two points clear of Nkana, who had gone top on Wednesday. Boyd Musonda put Blades ahead from the penalty spot in the 32nd minute and Idriss Ilunga Mbombo doubled the lead five minutes later from Biston Banda's assist; Sam Sikasote pulled one back for Trident in the 80th minute.

Power Dynamos beat NAPSA Stars 1–0 at the REIZ Arena in Lusaka with a 40th-minute strike from distance by Wilson Chisala, lifting Power to fifth on 10 points and leaving NAPSA ninth on four, without a win in six. Nchanga Rangers beat Makeni All Stars 3–1: Abraham Kanyangala opened the scoring in the 35th minute and Elliott Kampukesa added two in the second half, the first a minute after the restart and the second a 78th-minute penalty, before Joshua Chongo replied for Makeni in the 86th. Rangers are sixth on seven points; Makeni are bottom with one point, five defeats and 15 goals conceded in six games.

Green Eagles extended their lead at the top of Stream B to two points with a 2–0 win at Chirundu United, Derrick Bulaya scoring three minutes into the second half and again in the 56th minute. ZamFoot put Eagles on 14 points from six matches, four wins and two draws, with eight goals scored and one conceded, the best defensive record in the division; Chirundu are fourth on eight. The Lusaka derby at Sunset Stadium between Green Buffaloes and Zesco United finished 0–0. Paul Mbuyi was denied by Patrick Chooma in the 12th minute, Gift Mphande blocked a Buffaloes chance, and Abraham Siankombo headed over on the half hour. Buffaloes are second on 12 points; Zesco third on 10, with a goal difference of plus eight from ten scored and two conceded, from seven matches by ZamFoot's count. Mutondo Stars and Mufulira Wanderers drew 1–1: William Kamwanga scored for Wanderers in the 13th minute, following up after Melody Sintumfya saved a penalty, and Raphael Silwimba equalised on the hour. Wanderers have three points from six, all draws; Mutondo are bottom on two.

The round closes the league programme before the international break: the Chipolopolo play Burundi in Ndola on Friday 13 November and in Bujumbura on 17 November, and the provisional squad assembled in Ndola on Thursday, ZamFoot reported.

stories.title: A Nice midfielder, a Sheffield Wednesday forward and a point from two games: Burundi name 25 for the double-header against Zambia on 13 and 17 November
stories.excerpt: Burundi have named a 25-man squad for their two AFCON 2027 Group I qualifiers against Zambia, ZamFoot reported, led by OGC Nice midfielder Youssouf Ndayishimiye and including Sheffield Wednesday's Jordi Liongala and NAC Breda's Karim Mperanyi. Burundi are bottom of the group with one point after losing 1–0 to Togo and drawing 2–2 with Algeria in September; Zambia are second on three points, a point behind Algeria, and host the first leg at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November.

image.label: Group I, round three
image.caption: Burundi's squad for the Zambia double-header draws on clubs in Europe, north Africa and the Rwandan league.

body: The opponents for the Chipolopolo's next two matches have shown their hand. ZamFoot reported on Thursday 5 November that Burundi have announced a 25-man squad for the back-to-back Africa Cup of Nations 2027 Group I qualifiers against Zambia this month. Burundi go into the games bottom of the group with a single point, having lost 1–0 to Togo and drawn 2–2 with Algeria in September's opening two rounds, and ZamFoot described the meetings with Zambia as important for a side still looking for its first win of the campaign.

The squad has three goalkeepers, Daniel Hakizimana of Vision FC in Burundi and two based in Rwanda, Jonathan Nahimana of Gicumbi and Onésime Rukundo of Police FC. The eight defenders include Frederic Nsabiyumva of Västerås SK and Emmanuel Swedi of Nordic United in Sweden, Clauss Niyukuri of Sarpsborg 08 in Norway, Christophe Nduwarugira of PSS Sleman in Indonesia, and three more from Rwandan clubs. In midfield the best-known name is Youssouf Ndayishimiye of OGC Nice, alongside Gael Bigirimana of Dungannon, Mossi Nduwumwe of MC Alger, Henry Msanga of Al-Taawoun in Libya and Karim Mpawenimana of Costa do Sol in Mozambique. The eight forwards include Jordi Liongala of Sheffield Wednesday, Karim Mperanyi of NAC Breda, Bienvenue Kanakimana of Zbrojovka Brno, Mohamed Amissi of Vancouver FC and Caleb Bimenyimana of Al Karamah in Syria, with Franck Nduwimana of KCB in Kenya and Asman Ndikumana of Police FC. ZamFoot's report did not name the Burundi coach.

ZamFoot reported on Wednesday that the interim coach, George Lwandamina, had named a 30-man provisional squad, with four goalkeepers, ten defenders, eleven midfielders and five forwards, to be trimmed to 26, assembling in Ndola on Thursday with the foreign-based players joining when the FIFA window opens on 9 November. Chanka Zimba of Vitória de Sernache in Portugal was recalled, Zesco United's Kennedy Musonda and Gift Mphande were called up, and Red Arrows' Zephaniah Phiri, now fit, and Ackim Mumba were included. Some players were left out because they are with the Under-23s, who play Burkina Faso in Ouagadougou on 11 November and at Heroes Stadium four days later.

analysis.title: The budget's bet: a half-point of VAT now, a 3% deficit later
analysis.body: The 2027 budget raises the tax everyone pays and taxes the dividends the mines have not paid, and it does both to narrow a deficit that has drifted to an expected 5.9% of GDP against a 2.1% target. The government's case is that stabilisation is done and growth comes next: K284.8 billion, 82% of it from domestic revenue, with the borrowing share held to 14.7% and a path to 3% next year and 1.2% by 2029. The critics' case, put first by Fred M'membe, is that the burden lands on consumers through VAT, mobile money levies and a sugar tax while K67.6 billion goes to creditors, more than double what health receives. Three things decide which reading holds. First, whether the K10.8 billion the tax measures are meant to raise actually arrives, since a VAT rise can push trade into the informal sector. Second, copper: the deficit path assumes output rising past a million tonnes in 2027 after a 930,000-tonne year, and prices that have already touched US$14,000. Third, the rains, because the budget pre-funds a drought the government says it expects. The IMF's final approval, which Briefs, citing Bloomberg, reports hangs on the deficit goal, is the external judge.

analysis.title: What an observer report can and cannot do, and why Kalaba's question matters
analysis.body: Harry Kalaba's response to the EU mission, accept every finding and then ask what the observers intend to do about them, puts a question that both sides of Zambia's election argument have reason to answer. For the opposition and the church monitors, the report's 13 recommendations, on ZNBC airtime, the campaign timetable, police conduct and the suspension of counting, are a record they can hold up; but observers have no enforcement power, and Mr Kalaba's point that reports since 1996 have repeated themselves is hard to dispute. For the government, the answer it has given, that observers cannot see what the police and intelligence services can, is a reason to discount the findings on security, but it does not address the airtime or timetable findings, which rest on public data. What to watch is whether any recommendation becomes a bill, a broadcasting policy or an ECZ rule change before the next electoral cycle, and whether the parties that have now received the report, Citizens First first among them, put the recommendations to Parliament and the Commission in writing. The report's value will be measured in those documents, not in the week's statements.

analysis.title: A retirement without a reason, and the question it leaves the ministry
analysis.body: Dr Paul Chibwe's early retirement in the national interest is, on what has been published, an administrative act without a stated cause. Retirement in the national interest is a lawful instrument, and the ministry may have grounds it has not yet given; Mr M'membe's own statement lists other restructuring moves at the ministry and its agencies this year, and the budget has just promised 3,125 new health workers, so a reorganisation is one possible explanation. But the timing and the target invite the other reading, which Fred M'membe and Brian Mushimba have already given: that the president of the doctors' association, who spent the year pressing for the recruitment of volunteers already in the hospitals, has been removed for pressing. Two things would settle it. A written reason from the ministry or the Health Services Commission, which neither has given on any page read for this edition, and a clear statement of what happens to the association's recruitment demand now that its leader is outside the service. Until then the ministry carries the burden of the silence, and the doctors who were watching Dr Chibwe's case will draw their own conclusion about what speaking up costs.
